set_title: Microcytic anemia
stem: A 58-year-old woman with 20 years of rheumatoid arthritis has fatigue. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL, MCV is 78 fL, serum iron is low and ferritin is 350 ng/mL.
oneliner: 58F + 20 y rheumatoid arthritis + Hb 10.2 + MCV 78 + low iron + ferritin 350 → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her anemia?

whyNot.A: Iron deficiency has a **low ferritin**; hers is 350 ng/mL
whyNot.B: Thalassemia minor has a **normal serum iron**; hers is low, and it starts in childhood
whyNot.C: Lead gives **basophilic stippling** and an exposure history; she has neither, and her iron is low
whyNot.E: Sideroblastic anemia has a **high serum iron**; hers is low

why: Inflammation raises **hepcidin**, which locks iron inside macrophages: **serum iron falls while ferritin (stored iron) stays high**. Small cells come from the iron the marrow cannot reach.

set_title: Microcytic anemia
stem: A 24-year-old man has mild fatigue. Hemoglobin is 11.5 g/dL and MCV is 70 fL. The smear shows small, pale red cells. White cell and platelet counts are normal. Beta-thalassemia minor and iron deficiency anemia are both being considered.
oneliner: 24M + mild fatigue + Hb 11.5 + MCV 70 + small pale cells → thalassemia minor or iron deficiency?
ask: Which single finding favours beta-thalassemia minor over iron deficiency anemia?

options.B: Pale red cells on the smear

whyNot.A: A **low MCV** occurs in both; it is the shared finding that makes them look alike
whyNot.B: **Hypochromia** occurs in both: less hemoglobin in each cell
whyNot.D: A **mild anemia** fits both
whyNot.E: **White cells** are normal in both; neither condition touches them

why: With fewer beta chains, alpha chains pair with delta chains, so **hemoglobin A2 (α2δ2) rises above 3.5%**. Iron deficiency leaves A2 normal or low.

set_title: Transfusion reactions
stem: A 58-year-old man begins a unit of packed red cells. Fifteen minutes in, he has a temperature of 38.8°C, a pulse of 124/min and a blood pressure of 85/50 mm Hg. His urine is wine-colored.
oneliner: 58M + packed red cells + fever, tachycardia and hypotension at 15 min + wine-colored urine → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: A delayed reaction appears **3 to 10 days later** and is mild; his began 15 minutes in
whyNot.B: The IgA reaction brings **wheeze and cramps without fever**; he has fever and red urine
whyNot.D: An allergic urticarial reaction gives **only itching and hives**; he is febrile and hypotensive with red urine

stem: A 58-year-old man who was transfused 3 years ago receives 2 units of packed red cells. His hemoglobin then falls from 10.2 to 7.4 g/dL, he becomes mildly jaundiced and the direct Coombs test is positive. Acute and delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions are both being considered.

ask: Which single finding favours a delayed over an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?

options.B: Onset 7 days after an uneventful transfusion

whyNot.A: A **positive direct Coombs test** occurs in both, because antibody coats donor red cells in each
whyNot.C: **Indirect bilirubin** rises with hemolysis of either kind
whyNot.D: **Haptoglobin** falls in both as it binds released hemoglobin

why: An acute reaction comes from preformed anti-A or anti-B and starts within minutes. In a delayed reaction, **a prior transfusion sensitized him to a minor antigen, and memory IgG rises 3 to 10 days after re-exposure**, coating red cells for extravascular destruction.

set_title: Clots and pregnancy loss: antiphospholipid syndrome vs inherited thrombophilia
stem: A 31-year-old woman has swelling of the left leg from a deep vein thrombosis. Eighteen months ago she had a stillbirth at 21 weeks' gestation. She takes no medications. Platelet count and prothrombin time are normal. Her partial thromboplastin time is normal, and adding activated protein C to her plasma does not lengthen its clotting time.
oneliner: 31F + DVT + stillbirth at 21 weeks + normal aPTT + plasma resists activated protein C → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Antiphospholipid syndrome prolongs the **aPTT** through the lupus anticoagulant; hers is normal and her plasma resists activated protein C
whyNot.C: In protein C deficiency, **added activated protein C still works** on normal factor V; her plasma resists it

stem: A 34-year-old man has had two episodes of deep vein thrombosis. Platelet count and prothrombin time are normal and his father also had clots. Protein C deficiency and antithrombin deficiency are both considered.
oneliner: 34M + two DVTs + father with clots + normal platelets + normal PT → protein C or antithrombin deficiency?
ask: Which single finding favours protein C deficiency over antithrombin deficiency?

options.B: Normal platelet count and prothrombin time
options.C: Painful skin necrosis on days 3 to 5 of warfarin

whyNot.A: Both are **autosomal dominant venous thrombophilias**, so recurrence does not separate them
whyNot.B: Both leave **platelets and PT normal**
whyNot.D: Both are **inherited** and run in families
whyNot.E: Early thrombosis is a feature of **both**

why: Protein C has a **short half-life**, so warfarin lowers it before the other vitamin K factors and creates a transient hypercoagulable state with **skin necrosis**. Antithrombin deficiency instead shows **heparin resistance**.

set_title: Easy bleeding: platelets, von Willebrand factor or a clotting factor
stem: A 24-year-old woman has had heavy menstrual periods since menarche and frequent nosebleeds. Her father also has frequent nosebleeds. Platelet count is normal, bleeding time is prolonged, PT is normal, and aPTT is slightly prolonged.
oneliner: 24F + heavy periods since menarche + nosebleeds + father with nosebleeds + normal platelets + long bleeding time + normal PT + slightly long aPTT → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Hemophilia A leaves the bleeding time **normal** and bleeds into joints; she has **nosebleeds and a prolonged bleeding time**
whyNot.B: ITP needs a **low platelet count**; hers is **normal**
whyNot.D: Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the **PT**; hers is **normal**
whyNot.E: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) leaves the **bleeding time and aPTT normal**; hers are **prolonged and slightly prolonged**

why: Von Willebrand factor tethers platelets to damaged endothelium and carries factor VIII in plasma. When it is low, mucosal bleeding appears with a **normal platelet count and a prolonged bleeding time**, and the aPTT is slightly long because factor VIII is low. Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant, which fits an affected father.

stem: A 33-year-old woman has had 2 months of fatigue and episodes of dark urine that are darkest on waking. She has had no surgery and has never received a transfusion.
